4. The learned Advocate further contends that the Government of Bangladesh is under legal obligation not to extradite Anup Chetia to India. To support his contention he read out to us the following passages from International Law in Contemporary Perspective written by Myres Dougal W Michael Reisman from the case of Ramos vs. Diaz 1498 of the treatise: "The right of a foreign power to demand the extradition of one accused of crime and the correlative duty to surrender him exists only when created by treaty; and in the United States, in the absence of statutory or treaty provision therefor, no authority exists in any branch of the government to surrender a fugitive criminal to a foreign government: 

 ………………………………….……………………………………"Perhaps the leading case on the subject is In re Castioni (1891) 1 QB 149. In that case, the following pertinent comments are made: ............... Hawkins, J (165) .. . . . . . . . . . ... . .. .. I think, therefore that the expression in the Extradition Act ought (unless some better interpretation of it can be suggested) to be interpreted to mean that fugitive criminals are not to be surrendered for extradition crimes, if those crimes were incidental to and formed a part of political disturbances …………………" 

 The learned Advocate contends that the right to self-determination received judicial recognition in the cases of Namibia and Western Sahara. In support of his contention he quoted the following passage from his book Human Rights, Self-Determination and the Right to Resistance: The Case Study of Hawaii, 

 "Moreover, in his separate opinion in the Namibia Case, Judge Ammoun, citing statement by the representative of Pakistan, said that the "right of self-determination is a norm of the nature of jes cogens, derogation from which is not permissible under any circumstances". Judge Ammoun also referred to the principle of self-determination in his separate opinion in the Barcelona Traction Case: 

 Relying upon the above noted observation in the cases cited by him and the passages and Article of the Convention he submits that even if a member of a group is killed, that would amount to genocide. Therefore, if Anup Chetia is extradited to India Bangladesh shall be held responsible under Article III(b) and III(c) of the Convention. The right to life is a peremptory norm of International Law accepted and recognised by the International Community of States as a whole from which no derogation is permitted. Any derogation shall make the State an international delict. If Anup Chetia is extradited, Bangladesh shall also be in violation of Article 25 of the Bangladesh Constitution. He submits that Anup Chetia is to be treated as an internationally protected person and he has not committed any prejudicial act on the soil of Bangladesh. He further submits that notice is to be taken of the Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples (UNGA Res. 1514 XXXX (XV) (1960), and the Declaration on Friendly Relations and Co-operation Among States in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations, GA Res. 2625 (XXV), 25 UNGAOR, Supp. (No. 28). He also submits that the right to self-determination has evolved as the seven principles on International Law, and has been recognised in the Namibia case (1971) and the Western Sahara (1975) case by the World Court as has been noted in the Connecticut Journal of International Law, Vol. 5, Spring, 1990, No.2. It was also recognised as an imperative rule of law in the cases of Barcelona Traction, Light and Power Co. (1970) by the World Court. 

 5. Before we enter upon discussion on merit of the case we propose to consider the question of maintainability of this petition. In Dr Mohiuddin Faruk the petitioner as a public spirited person filed the writ petition for protection of the right to life guaranteed under Article 32 of our Constitution to espouse the cause of members of the public. The facts of that case are that the petitioner Dr Mohiuddin Faruk was the Secretary-General of the Bangladesh Environmental Lawyers' Association, shortly called BELA. The said organisation has been contributing to maintain balance in the field of environment and ecology of Bangladesh. In that writ petition the implementation of Flood Action Programme, FAP-20 was impugned on the ground that such implementation would adversely affect more than a million human lives and natural resources and the natural habitat of man and other flora and fauna in the District of Tangail and the adjacent area, which aroused wide attention as implementation of the Programme is anti-environment and anti-people project. The petitioner further stated in the petition that the BELA conducted investigations at various times from 1992-93 in the FAP-20 areas. He alleged that no proper environmental impact assessment had been undertaken in relation to the FAP projects although the European Parliament declared in its resolution of 24 June 1993 that there was urgent need of changing the FAP's classification within the World Bank .project scheme from category 'B' to category 'A' requiring full environmental assessment A group of environmental lawyers possessed of pertinent, bonafide and well recognised expertise contributed in the field of environment and having dedicated and established status moved the writ petition for a judicial review of certain activities under FAP under- taken with foreign assistance on the grounds, inter alia, that implementation of the programme will cause environmental degradation and ecological imbalance in the district of Tangail and adjacent areas in violation of the law. The petitioner argued before the High Court Division that he is a person aggrieved as contemplated under Article 102(1) of the Constitution of People's Republic of Bangladesh. The High Court Division, however, negatived his contention holding that he is not a "person aggrieved" and summarily rejected the writ petition. The petitioner took an appeal to the Appellate Division. But the Appellate Division held that the petitioner is an aggrieved person. The learned Advocate for the petitioner before us relying upon the referred observation, para 96, of the case of Dr Mohiuddin Faruk contends that the present petitioner who is also a Secretary-General of the Human Rights Commission of Bangladesh is a "person aggrieved" within the meaning of Article 102(1) of the Constitution like the petitioner in Dr Mohiuddin Faruk as his "heart bleeds" for Anup Chetia who is espousing the cause of the Assamese people for self-determination. At paragraph 96 of the report the Appellate Division observed: "In such harrowing conditions of our people in general if socially conscious and public spirited persons are not allowed to approach the Court on behalf of the public or a section thereof for enforcement of their rights the very scheme of the Constitution will be frustrated The inescapable conclusion therefore. is that the expression "person aggrieved" means not only any person who is personally aggrieved but also one whose heart bleeds for his less fortunate fellow beings for a wrong done by the government or a local authority not fulfilling its Constitutional or statutory obligations. It does not however extend to a person who is an interpolar and interferes with things which do not concern him. This approach is in keeping with the Constitutional principles that are being evolved in the recent times in different Countries." 

 The aforequoted observation does not help the learned Advocate. First, there is no statement in the petition that Anup Chetia is "a less fortunate follow." of the petition. Nowhere within the four corners of the petition it is stated that Anup Chetia is also unable to vindicate his own right. Secondly, no wrong has been done by the Government or a local authority of Bangladesh in not fulfilling its Constitutional or statutory obligation to the petitioner. Thirdly, from the statement made in this petition we do not find that the petitioner or his organisation has been contributing to the cause of people like that of the BELA. Merely because one is a Secretary-General or a member of any Human Rights Organisation is not sufficiant ground to hold that he has a sufficient interest in the field. Where a writ petitioner fails to bring anything on record to satisfy the court that he consistently has been endeavouring to obtain remedy for a section or group of people in the event of violation or threatened violation of their any legal or constitutional rights whose abject poverty, illiteracy and socially disadvantaged position bar access to Court for redress of injustice, and the petitioner or his organisation fails to satisfy that he or his organisation has contributed in order to secure justice or to restore or enforce any of the human rights in the field for which he has been espousing cause of those persons in the Court of law as a public spirited person such person or organisation cannot be said to be a "person aggrieved" within the meaning of Article 102(1) of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh for lack of sufficient interest in the field. In this petition we find no such statement regarding the activities of the petitioner in the related field. Anup Chetia was charged with treason in his own country for leading, his people for "self-determination." Can the Court hold that the petitioner is a "person aggrieved" by stretching the meaning of the expression "person aggrieved" only because his "heart bleeds" for handing over Anup Chetia to Indian authority from reading news published in the newspaper. We refrain ourselves from taking such view by stretching the meaning of "person aggrieved" and hold that the petitioner has no locus standi to maintain this petition as he is not an aggrieved person. This view of ours finds support from the following observation made by the learned Chief Justice in Dr Mohiuddin Faruk's Case. The learned Chief Justice observed: 

 "A person pleading sufficient interest may be able to cross; what is called, the threshold stage on the averments made in the writ petition but it will always remain open for a prospective respondent to contest the said claim on facts and also to assail the bonafides or even the appropriateness in a, particular case of the petitioner for seeking a relief invoking the Constitutional jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution. For example, standing was denied to the Bangladesh Sangbad Patra Parishad to represent its opulent members, namely, the newspaper owners who were directly affected by the Wage Board A ward but even then none of them moved personally, but the Consideration would have been different if any organisation representing a weaker section of the Society had come to complain about a breach of any fundamental right of its members or any public wrong done to the members generally in breach of any provision of the constitution or law. The Court will have to decide in each, particularly when objection is taken, not only the extent of sufficiency of interest but also the fitness of the person for invoking the discretionary jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution. Ordinarily, it is the affected party which is to come to the Court for remedy. The Court is considering the question of the standing in a particular case if the affected party is not before it will enquire as to why the affected party is not coming before it and if it finds no satisfactory reason for non-appearance of the affected party it may refuse to entertain the application. 

 6. As this case is of first impression we are inclined to consider the contention raised at the Bar on merit. Before we examine the decisions and the views expressed in the case relied upon by the learned Advocate for the petitioner we want to examine the law and the Constitutional position obtaining in our country. The learned Advocate relying upon Articel25 of our Constitution contended that Anup Chetia, if extradited to India the Government would violate the mandate of Article 25. The contention on the facts of this case is totally misconceived. Rather the Government can take help of Article 25 for the purpose to extradite Anup Chetia to Indian authority in order to base its international relations on the principle of 'respect for national sovereignty and equality, non-interference in the internal affairs of other countries. True, that fundamental principle of state policy, here Article 25, can not be enforced by Court, nevertheless the fundamental principles of state policy is fundamental to the governance of Bangladesh, and serve as a tool in interpreting the Constitution and other laws of Bangladesh on the strength of Article 8(2) of the Constitution by the superior Court. Article 25(1)(c) enjoins upon the state to support oppressed people throughout the world waging a just struggle against imperialism, colonialism or racialism. We are afraid to accept the contention that as because Anup Chetia is struggling for "self-determination" for the people of Assam handing over him to India would be violative of Article 25 of our Constitution. The struggle in which ULFA and its Secretary-General Anup Chetia is involved is not in our opinion "waging a just struggle against imperialism, colonialism or racialism." The petitioner in this petition states "That Mr Chetia is the Secretary-General of the Liberation Front of Assam (ULFA) the party leading the liberation struggle of the Assamese people." It is difficult for us to view" Liberation struggle of the Assamese People" as "struggle against imperialism, colonialism or racialism" the expressions employed in Article 25 (l)(c) of the Constitution of People's Republic of Bangladesh. Nor can. it be said that right to "self-determination" as canvassed in this petition falls within any of the three expressions viz, "imperialism", "colonialism or "racialism" as used in article 25(1)(c) in our Constitution. In this context we ourselves are inclined to refer to the decision in the case of M Saleemullah vs. Government of Bangladesh, 47 DLR 218 to which one of us is a party. The facts of that case are that the Government took the decision to participate in the UN sponsored Multinational Force to Haiti to help maintain public safety and basic civil order after restoration of the legitimately elected Government of Haiti under the UN Security Council's Resolution No. 940. The petitioner stated that the Bangladesh Observer also published news under the caption "Ghali asks army rulers to quit-US aircraft carrier ready to sail for invasion of Haiti, "and that the State Department announced in Washington that seventeen countries including three NATO allies and Bangladesh have pledged a combined minimum of 1500 troops to assist a US-led invasion of Haiti and the administration has been pushing hard to recruit troops to join America to oust Haiti's military dictatorship and the Haiti leaders have announced that they would counteract the foreign aggression. The petitioner further stated that the decision was taken during the Autumn Session of the Jatiya Sangsad (parliament) to join "US led invasion" without the assent of the parliament and during the boycott of the Parliament by the leaders of the opposition parties. The petitioner also alleged that the decision is against the Fundamental Principle of State Policy and the Fundamental Rights as envisaged in our Constitution and for the decision to send troops of Bangladesh to participate in US-led war of aggression in Haiti there must exist a grave emergency to the satisfaction of the President that the security or economic life of Bangladesh or any part thereof is threatened by war or external aggression or internal disturbance. In that case of M Saleemullah the learned Judges have observed: 

 7. Now, it remains for us to consider the case cited from foreign jurisdiction. At the outset we must say that observations made therein are pious expression to secure international fundamental human right, norms obtaining in different declarations and covenants of different state parties to such instrument and have little binding force on the municipal Courts. Such views no doubt have opened a new horizon of International Human Right law but in international human rights law interpretation adopted by national courts can at best only be persuasive authority. In Ramoz vs. Diaz, the right of a foreign power to demand the extradition was created by treaty. And in US in absence of statutory or treaty provision no authority exists in the Government to surrender a fugitive criminal to a foreign Government. A careful reading of the judgment will show that the decision rests on Article VI of the treaty of Extradition made between Government of the US and the Government of Cuba. Article VI of the treaty exempts extradition of a fugitive charged with political offence from the treaty. But Extradition Act, 1974 of our country does not provide such exemption. Therefore, the decision which is only of a persuasive value and decided placing reliance upon Article VI of the Extradition Treaty has no manner of application to the facts of the instant case. Let us now examine the contention whether in absence of any extradition treaty between Bangladesh and the Union of India the Government can extradite Anup Chetia to India. In this regard relevant law is to be found in section 4 of the Extradition Act, 1974 of Bangladesh. Section 4 reads: 

 8. Now let us consider section 3(1) of the Special Powers Act, 1974. Section 3(1) of the Act empowers the Government to make an order directing any person to remove himself from Bangladesh in such a manner as it may specify in the order in order to prevent him from doing any prejudicial act. Section 2(f) has given meaning of the expression "prejudicial act". According to section 2 (f)(ii) "prejudical act", amongst others, means "act to prejudice the maintenance of friendly relations of Bangladesh with foreign States." Thus, in a case where a citizen of a foreign country intends to stay in Bangladesh and if the Government is satisfied that extradition of such person is called for in order to maintain friendly relations of Bangladesh with foreign States the Government can on the strength of section 3(1) and section 2(f)(ii) of the Special Powers Act, 1974 extradite such citizen to his own country in absence of any extradition treaty between the government of Bangladesh and such foreign States. Thus, reading section 4 of the Extradition Act, 1974 and section 3(1) read with section 2(f)(ii) together, we hold that the government of Bangladesh has sufficient legal authority to extradite Anup Chetia to India in response to the right of India to demand extradition of Anup Chetia.
